name: Jealous Breast (Du Ru)
description: Jealous Breast (Du Ru) (Dù Rǔ, 妒乳) is a full TCM pattern. Key signs: Breast distension and hardness, Severe breast pain worsening with touch, High fever. Rel...

timing_worsening_explanation: This condition occurs exclusively in the postpartum period, typically within the first few days to weeks after delivery. It is most likely to develop when the newborn is unable to nurse effectively, when milk first comes in strongly, or when feeding is interrupted. Symptoms tend to worsen at night when feedings may be less frequent. The condition can progress rapidly from initial engorgement to full abscess within days if milk stasis is not resolved. Fever tends to spike in the afternoon and evening, consistent with the general pattern of heat conditions worsening in the yang portion of the day.
practitioner_notes:
Diagnosing Jealous Breast (Du Ru) rests on recognizing a specific clinical scenario: a recently postpartum woman whose breast milk has failed to flow properly, leading to a cascade of local congestion, heat, and pain. The classical texts describe this mechanism clearly: when a newborn cannot nurse, or when milk is not fully expressed, the milk accumulates inside the breast and 'struggles' with the body's Qi and Blood. This struggle generates heat, which manifests as high fever, intense thirst, and a breast so painful that it cannot be touched.
The diagnostic reasoning follows a clear logic. First, the timing must be postpartum. Second, there must be evidence of milk stasis: the breast is swollen and hard, milk does not flow freely. Third, signs of heat must be present: fever, thirst, a red tongue with yellow coating, and a rapid pulse. The classical physician Chen Ziming explained that Chui Nai (simple breast engorgement), Du Ru (milk stasis with heat), and Ru Yong (breast abscess) are fundamentally the same condition at different stages of severity. Du Ru sits in the middle, where simple engorgement has not yet become a pus-filled abscess but has already developed heat and significant pain. This staging is critical for treatment: catching the condition at the Du Ru stage and vigorously clearing the milk can prevent progression to abscess.
The underlying organ systems involved are the Stomach and the Liver. In TCM theory, the breast belongs to the Stomach channel (Zu Yangming), while the nipple is governed by the Liver channel. Breast milk itself is considered a transformation of Qi and Blood, nourished through the Chong and Ren extraordinary vessels and distributed via the Stomach channel. When the Liver fails to maintain the smooth flow of Qi (often due to emotional upset after delivery), and when the Stomach channel accumulates heat (often from rich food), the milk cannot circulate and stagnates, setting the stage for Du Ru.
pathophysiology: Breast milk stagnates in the ducts after childbirth, combining with Qi stagnation and Heat to cause painful breast swelling that can progress to abscess if untreated.
treatment_principle: Promote lactation and unblock the breast ducts, soothe the Liver and clear Heat, disperse swelling and relieve pain
typical_timeline: 3-7 days for mild cases with prompt treatment, 1-3 weeks if moderate swelling and Heat are present. Early intervention is critical to prevent abscess formation.
formula_modifications:
If the breast is very swollen and hard with sharp pain: Add Chi Shao (red peony) and Ru Xiang (frankincense) to invigorate Blood and reduce swelling more forcefully.
If there is high fever and strong thirst: Add Shi Gao (gypsum) and Zhi Mu (anemarrhena) to clear intense Heat from the Stomach channel, as described in the classical use of Shi Gao San for internal breast abscess.
If the person feels very stressed, irritable, and emotionally upset: Add Xiang Fu (cyperus) and Yu Jin (curcuma tuber) to more strongly move Liver Qi and relieve emotional constraint.
If the breast milk is very scanty or does not flow at all: Add Wang Bu Liu Xing (vaccaria seed) and Tong Cao (rice paper pith) to strongly promote lactation and open the milk ducts.
If the breast is beginning to form pus (indicating progression toward abscess): Add Zao Jiao Ci (gleditsia thorn) and Chuan Shan Jia (pangolin scale, where legal alternatives are available) to break through toxicity and promote drainage. At this stage, stronger intervention is needed.
If the person feels fatigued and weak postpartum: Add Huang Qi (astragalus) and Dang Gui (Chinese angelica) to support Qi and Blood. Deficiency can underlie the stagnation, and tonification helps the body resolve the condition from within.

causes_details: [{"cause_title": "Breast milk accumulation (乳汁蓄积)", "explanation": "This is the most direct and common cause. After giving birth, breast milk is produced in abundance. If the baby cannot latch properly, if the mother does not nurse frequently enough, or if the milk ducts become blocked for any reason, the milk accumulates inside the breast. In TCM, when any fluid stagnates in the body it generates Heat over time, much like standing water grows warm and stagnant. The accumulated milk mixes with Qi and Blood in the breast channels, creating congestion, swelling, hardness, and pain. The classical texts describe this very clearly: Ge Hong wrote that when breast milk cannot be discharged, it collects internally and this is called Du Ru, and that it is more urgent than a simple abscess."}, {"cause_title": "Liver Qi stagnation from emotional upset (肝气郁结)", "explanation": "The postpartum period is an emotionally vulnerable time. Frustration, worry, sadness, or anger can all cause the Liver to lose its ability to keep Qi flowing smoothly. In TCM, the Liver system governs the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body, and the nipple specifically belongs to the Liver channel. When the Liver becomes constrained, Qi stops moving freely through the breast ducts, and the milk cannot flow out. This stagnation creates distension and pain in the breast, often accompanied by a feeling of tightness in the chest, sighing, and mood swings. Classical physicians like Zhu Danxi specifically noted that anger and emotional suppression obstruct the Liver channel, blocking the breast ducts and leading to breast swelling and abscess."}, {"cause_title": "Stomach Heat from rich diet (胃热壅盛)", "explanation": "In many cultures, new mothers are encouraged to eat rich, nourishing foods after delivery. While nourishment is important, excessive consumption of greasy, fatty, sweet, or spicy foods can generate Heat in the Stomach system. In TCM, the breast belongs to the Stomach channel (Foot Yangming), and Stomach Heat rises directly into the breast tissue. This Heat thickens the breast milk, makes it sluggish, and causes the breast ducts to become inflamed and swollen. The Wai Ke Zheng Zong specifically mentions that rich diet and Liver fire acting together are common causes of breast swelling and abscess formation."}, {"cause_title": "Improper breastfeeding technique or nipple damage", "explanation": "Physical factors play an important role. If the baby's latch is poor, if breastfeeding is infrequent or inconsistent, or if the nipple becomes cracked or injured, the normal pathway for milk drainage is disrupted. Cracked nipples can also allow external pathogens (what Western medicine would call bacteria) to enter the breast tissue. In TCM terms, broken skin allows Wind-Heat or toxic pathogens to invade through the damaged surface, adding a layer of Heat toxicity to the underlying milk stagnation. The combination of internal stagnation and external invasion accelerates progression toward abscess."}]

formulas.name: Gua Lou Niu Bang Zi Tang
formulas.description: Gua Lou Niu Bang Zi Tang (Trichosanthes and Arctium Decoction) is the most representative formula for early-stage breast abscess and Du Ru. It clears Heat, disperses swelling, unblocks the breast ducts, and promotes lactation. It is used when Heat toxins are accumulating and the breast is swollen, hard, and painful.

formulas.name: Xiao Yao San
formulas.description: Xiao Yao San (Free and Easy Wanderer) is used when Liver Qi stagnation is the dominant mechanism, with emotional upset, breast distension, irritability, and sighing. It soothes the Liver, strengthens the Spleen, and helps restore smooth Qi flow through the breast.

formulas.name: Ju Ye San
formulas.description: Ju Ye San (Tangerine Leaf Powder), from the Wai Ke Zheng Zong, is specifically indicated for breast swelling from rich diet and Liver fire causing breast nodules. It disperses Qi stagnation and resolves Phlegm-Heat in the breast.

formulas.name: Wu Zhu Yu Tang
formulas.description: Dan Zhu Ye Tang (Bland Bamboo Leaf Decoction), recorded in the Liu Juanzi Gui Yi Fang, is one of the earliest formulas for treating Du Ru and breast abscess, clearing Heat and promoting milk flow.

herbs.name: Pu Gong Ying
herbs.description: Dandelion (Pu Gong Ying) clears Heat and resolves toxicity, is a key herb for breast disorders. It reduces swelling and helps resolve early-stage breast inflammation.

herbs.name: Gua Lou
herbs.description: Trichosanthes fruit (Gua Lou) clears Heat, resolves Phlegm, and disperses breast nodules. It broadens the chest and helps move stagnation in the breast area.

herbs.name: Niu Bang Zi
herbs.description: Arctium seed (Niu Bang Zi) disperses Wind-Heat and reduces swelling. It is especially useful for breast pain with swelling and is a principal herb in Niu Bang Zi Tang for breast abscess.

herbs.name: Wang Bu Liu Xing
herbs.description: Vaccaria seed (Wang Bu Liu Xing) invigorates Blood and promotes lactation. It is one of the most important herbs for unblocking breast milk flow.

herbs.name: Lu Lu Tong
herbs.description: Liquidambar fruit (Lu Lu Tong) promotes the flow of Qi and Blood through the channels, helping to open obstructed breast ducts.

herbs.name: Chai Hu
herbs.description: Bupleurum (Chai Hu) soothes Liver Qi and resolves stagnation. Liver Qi stagnation is a core mechanism in Du Ru, and Chai Hu helps restore the Liver's role in regulating breast milk flow.

herbs.name: Qing Pi
herbs.description: Green tangerine peel (Qing Pi) breaks up stagnant Qi in the Liver channel and is specific for breast distension and pain. It enters the Liver channel and directly addresses the breast area.

herbs.name: Jin Yin Hua
herbs.description: Honeysuckle (Jin Yin Hua) clears Heat and resolves toxicity. When there is early-stage Heat or the threat of infection, it helps prevent progression to abscess.

herbs.name: Si Gua Luo
herbs.description: Loofah sponge (Si Gua Luo) unblocks the channels and collaterals, particularly in the breast. It is a traditional remedy specifically for promoting breast milk flow and relieving breast distension.

herbs.name: Lian Qiao
herbs.description: Forsythia fruit (Lian Qiao) clears Heat, reduces swelling, and disperses nodules. It is commonly paired with Jin Yin Hua for breast conditions with Heat.

acupoints.name: Shaoze SI-1
acupoints.description: SI-1 (Shaoze) is the most important empirical point for all breast disorders. It promotes lactation, clears Heat, and unblocks the breast ducts. It can be needled or bled with a lancet to release Heat.

acupoints.name: Shanzhong REN-17
acupoints.description: REN-17 (Danzhong) is the influential point of Qi, located at the center of the chest. It regulates Qi in the chest and breast area, relieves breast distension, and promotes the smooth flow of breast milk.

acupoints.name: Rugen ST-18
acupoints.description: ST-18 (Rugen) is a local point directly below the breast. It is indicated for all breast conditions including mastitis, breast pain, and insufficient lactation. It helps move stagnation locally.

acupoints.name: Jianjing GB-21
acupoints.description: GB-21 (Jianjing) strongly moves Qi and Blood downward through the chest, promotes lactation, and is a key empirical point for breast engorgement and milk let-down difficulties.

acupoints.name: Zusanli ST-36
acupoints.description: ST-36 (Zusanli) tonifies the Stomach and Spleen, the source of Qi and Blood that produces breast milk. It supports overall postnatal recovery and ensures adequate nourishment reaches the breast.

acupoints.name: Taichong LR-3
acupoints.description: LIV-3 (Taichong) soothes Liver Qi stagnation, the root cause of many Du Ru presentations. It relieves emotional constraint and helps restore the smooth flow of Qi through the breast.

acupoints.name: Qimen LR-14
acupoints.description: LIV-14 (Qimen) is the Front-Mu point of the Liver, located on the chest. It is especially useful for Liver Qi stagnation affecting the breast and chest, relieving fullness, distension, and pain in the breast area.

faqs.question: What is Jealous Breast (Du Ru) in TCM?
faqs.answer: Breast milk stagnates in the ducts after childbirth, combining with Qi stagnation and Heat to cause painful breast swelling that can progress to abscess if untreated.

faqs.question: What are the key signs of Jealous Breast (Du Ru)?
faqs.answer: Key signs include: Breast distension and hardness, Severe breast pain worsening with touch, High fever, Strong thirst with desire to drink, Pulling or tugging pain in the breast, Redness and warmth of the breast skin, Breast milk that is difficult to express, Irritability and restlessness, Chills alternating with fever, Nausea or vomiting.

faqs.question: What formulas treat Jealous Breast (Du Ru)?
faqs.answer: Common formulas for Jealous Breast (Du Ru) include: Gua Lou Niu Bang Zi Tang, Xiao Yao San, Ju Ye San, Wu Zhu Yu Tang.

faqs.question: What Western conditions relate to Jealous Breast (Du Ru)?
faqs.answer: This pattern is associated with: Acute lactation mastitis, Breast engorgement, Blocked milk duct, Breast abscess (early stage).

faqs.question: What is the treatment principle for Jealous Breast (Du Ru)?
faqs.answer: Promote lactation and unblock the breast ducts, soothe the Liver and clear Heat, disperse swelling and relieve pain
